d.t: Any member of a race of beings from (especially Scandinavian and other Germanic) folklore, usually depicted as having some sort of supernatural powers and being skilled in crafting and metalworking, often as short with long beards, and sometimes as clashing with elves.
d.e: [T]he elf king and his queen made a royal progress every noon with a splendid retinue of dwarves and sprites, […]

d.t: A person of short stature, often one whose limbs are disproportionately small in relation to the body as compared with typical adults, usually as the result of a genetic condition.
d.e: The nurse exclaimed it when I finally arrived, a month late (a habit I have kept). That's how my parents found out that I was a little person, a dwarf, of short stature.

d.t: An animal, plant or other thing much smaller than the usual of its sort.
d.e: dwarf tree

d.t: A dwarf star.
d.e: But none of those brown dwarfs were speeding along on a trajectory that would carry them out of the galaxy like “runaway” hypervelocity stars observed by astronomers in the last two decades. […] The study team said it’s likely the star was a companion to a white dwarf star, which…

d.t: Miniature.
d.e: The specimen is a very dwarf form of the plant.

d.t: To render (much) smaller, turn into a dwarf (version).
To make appear (much) smaller, puny, tiny; to be much larger than.
d.e: The newly-built skyscraper dwarfs all older buildings in the downtown skyline.

d.t: To make appear insignificant.
d.e: Bach dwarfs all other composers.

d.t: To become (much) smaller.
To hinder from growing to the natural size; to make or keep small; to stunt.
d.e: At present the whole sex is in a manner dwarfed and shrunk - into a race of beauties that seems almost another species

d.t: The situation where something is made to seem (relatively) small or unimportant.
d.e: Such intentional dwarfings of the human figure can carry different political valences, depending on the work that frames them.

d.t: Like a dwarf; being especially small or stunted.
d.e: […] now does he feel his title / Hang loose about him, like a giant's robe / Upon a dwarfish thief.

d.t: Of, pertaining to, or made by or for dwarves.
d.e: Dwarfish axes are some of the finest weapons available.

d.t: The condition of being a dwarf (person of short stature).
d.e: Studies of disproportionate dwarfisms in animals have revealed the importance of core proteins an sulfation in the development of cartilage.

d.t: The quality of being puny or inferior.
d.e: Childish, childish to the core: that's why they're so good at nursing, they're arrested in a state of permanent intellectual dwarfism themselves!

d.t: Similar to a dwarf, for example in stature.
Of, pertaining to, or made by or for dwarfs/dwarves.
A boring, studious, or socially inept person.
d.e: I may be dumb, but I'm not a dweeb.

d.t: Like, or characteristic of, a dweeb; nerdy, uncool.
d.e: THEY have no shame. That's my first reaction upon hearing that Candlestick Park has been violated by some dweeby Silicon Valley techno-name.

d.t: A period of time in which a system or component remains in a given state.
A brief pause in the motion of part of a mechanism to allow an operation to be completed.
A planned delay in a timed control program.

In a petrol engine, the period of time the ignition points are closed to let current flow through the ignition coil in between each spark. This is measured as an angle in degrees around the camshaft in the distributor which controls the points, for example in a 4-cylinder engine it might be 55° (spark at 90° intervals, points closed for 55° between each).
To live; to reside.
d.e: I am fully resolved to go dwell in another house.

d.t: To linger (on); to remain fixated.
d.e: Stop dwelling on the past!

d.t: To be in a given state.
To abide; to remain; to continue.
d.e: My liefe (ſayd ſhe) ye know, that long ygo, / Whileſt ye in durance dwelt, ye to me gaue / A little mayde, the which ye chylded tho ; / The ſame againe if now ye liſt to haue, / The ſame is yonder Lady, whom high God did ſaue.

d.t: An inhabitant of a specific place; an inhabitant or denizen.
d.e: The new couple are apartment dwellers.

d.t: A house or place in which a person lives; a habitation, a home.
d.e: The old house served as a dwelling for Albert.

d.t: A vector drawing file generated with AutoCAD.
To decrease, shrink, diminish, reduce in size or intensity.
d.e: Their supplies began to dwindle after a week.

d.t: To fall away in quality; degenerate, sink.
d.e: VVearie Seu'nights, nine times nine, / Shall he dvvindle, peake, and pine: […]

d.t: To lessen; to bring low.
d.e: Our drooping days are dwindled down to nought.

d.t: To break up or disperse.
d.e: there were only five hundred foot and three hundred horse left with him, for the blocking of Plymouth; the rest were dwindled away

d.t: Various health problems and frailty observed in elderly people.
declining; growing less
d.e: There is dwindling support for New Labour.

d.t: A gradual reduction to nothing.
A numerical value of twice the magnitude of a word, typically used in the same contexts as the fossilized 16-bit sense of "word" and thus 32 bits.
d.e: Using a double loop, each dword of the first factor is multiplied by each dword of the second factor […]
